title: Trinidadian Doubles with Curried Chickpeas & Tamarind Sauce
dek: Soft turmeric bara cradle saucy curried chickpeas, quick tamarind chutney and cool cucumber in a practical six-serving version of Trinidad’s beloved street food.
image_alt: Trinidad doubles with turmeric-yellow bara, saucy curried chickpeas, cucumber and chutneys served on brown paper
ingredients: 2 1/2 cups (300 g) all-purpose flour, plus up to 2 tablespoons more if needed
1 cup plus 2 tablespoons warm water (100 to 110°F), plus more by the teaspoon if needed
1 tablespoon neutral oil, plus more for shaping
4 cups neutral high-heat oil, such as canola or vegetable oil, for frying
1 packed tablespoon finely chopped culantro (chadon beni) or 2 tablespoons chopped cilantro, divided
1/2 English cucumber, coarsely grated and lightly squeezed

instructions.name: Mix a soft bara dough
instructions.text: Whisk the flour, yeast, 1 teaspoon brown sugar, 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/2 teaspoon turmeric in a large bowl. Pour in the warm water and mix with your fingers or a sturdy spoon until no dry flour remains. Knead in the bowl for 2 minutes; the dough should be very soft and tacky, not pourable. If it is dry, work in water 1 teaspoon at a time; if it will not hold together, add flour 1 tablespoon at a time. Rub with 1 tablespoon oil, cover and rest in a warm place for 30 minutes, until relaxed and slightly puffy.

instructions.name: Bloom the curry base
instructions.text: While the dough rests, heat 1 tablespoon of the frying oil in a 3-quart saucepan over medium. Add 1 1/2 tablespoons curry powder, 1 teaspoon cumin and the remaining 1/4 teaspoon turmeric. Stir for 30 seconds, just until fragrant. Add the garlic and cook for 20 seconds without browning.

instructions.name: Simmer the channa until spoon-soft
instructions.text: Add the chickpeas, baking soda, 1 1/2 cups water and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Bring to a lively simmer, then cook uncovered for 18 to 22 minutes, stirring and lightly crushing about one-quarter of the chickpeas against the pan. When the chickpeas are very tender and suspended in a thick, spoonable gravy, stir in half the culantro. Add hot water a tablespoon at a time if the channa tightens before the bara are ready; it should spread rather than sit in a dry mound.

instructions.name: Cook the quick tamarind chutney
instructions.text: In a small saucepan, whisk the tamarind concentrate, 3 tablespoons brown sugar, the remaining 1/2 tablespoon curry powder, remaining 1/2 teaspoon cumin and 1/4 cup water. Simmer over medium-low for 5 to 7 minutes, until glossy and thin enough to drizzle. Remove from the heat, stir in the lime juice and cool. It will thicken as it stands; loosen with water by the teaspoon if necessary.

instructions.name: Portion and stretch the bara
instructions.text: Lightly oil a sheet pan, your hands and a small section of the counter. Divide the rested dough into 12 equal pieces, about 41 g each, and roll into smooth balls. Cover for 10 minutes. Working with one ball at a time, press and gently stretch it into a thin 5-inch round; keep the center no thicker than 1/8 inch. Place the rounds on the oiled pan without stacking and keep loosely covered.

instructions.name: Fry at a controlled temperature
instructions.text: Pour the frying oil into a wide, heavy pot to a depth of about 1 inch and clip on a frying thermometer. Heat over medium-high to 350°F. Slide in one bara away from you; fry for 15 to 25 seconds per side, spooning a little hot oil over the top, until flexible, lightly puffed and cooked through but not crisp or deeply browned. Drain on a wire rack set over a sheet pan. Return the oil to 350 to 365°F between pieces and fry the remaining bara. Never let the oil exceed 375°F.

instructions.name: Hold the breads soft
instructions.text: As each bara finishes draining for about 30 seconds, transfer it to a clean towel-lined bowl and cover loosely with another towel. This trapped warmth keeps the thin breads pliable. If a bara snaps when folded, reduce the frying time by 5 seconds for the next batch.

instructions.name: Season the cool topping
instructions.text: Toss the squeezed cucumber with the remaining culantro and a small pinch of salt. Taste the channa and tamarind chutney separately; the chickpeas should be savory and earthy, while the chutney should be distinctly sweet-sour. Adjust with salt, lime or a teaspoon of water before assembling.

instructions.name: Build each double
instructions.text: For each serving, overlap two warm bara on a square of parchment or brown paper. Spoon about 1/2 cup hot channa across the center, drizzle with 1 to 2 teaspoons tamarind chutney and finish with cucumber and pepper sauce to taste. Fold the paper around the edges and serve immediately so the bara absorb some gravy without becoming sodden.

why_it_works: A very soft, briefly rested dough stretches thin without springing back, producing tender bara that stay flexible after their quick fry.
Blooming the curry powder in oil dissolves fat-soluble aromas before water and chickpeas enter the pan.
A pinch of baking soda accelerates chickpea softening; crushing only part of the batch thickens the gravy while leaving recognizable chickpeas.
Holding the oil between 350 and 365°F cooks the thin dough quickly without turning it cracker-crisp or letting it soak up excessive oil.
Tamarind, cool cucumber and optional pepper sauce provide the sweet, sour, fresh and hot contrasts that keep the rich fried bread and channa balanced.
swaps: If Caribbean curry powder is unavailable, mix 1 tablespoon ground coriander, 2 teaspoons ground cumin, 1 teaspoon turmeric, 1/2 teaspoon fenugreek and 1/2 teaspoon allspice; use 2 tablespoons of this blend.
Culantro has a deeper herbal flavor than cilantro, but cilantro is the most practical substitute. Use twice as much cilantro and add it only at the end.
For a milder family batch, omit pepper sauce from the filling and serve it at the table. Scotch bonnet sauce should be added drop by drop, not measured by the spoonful.
Tamarind paste strengths vary. If using a thick unsweetened paste rather than pourable concentrate, start with 2 tablespoons and increase only after tasting.
For a partially whole-grain bara, replace no more than 1/2 cup of the all-purpose flour with white whole-wheat flour and expect to add 1 to 2 tablespoons extra water.
storage: Doubles are best assembled and eaten immediately. Refrigerate channa and tamarind chutney separately in airtight containers within 2 hours; use channa within 4 days and chutney within 7 days. Cool leftover bara completely, layer with parchment and refrigerate for up to 2 days or freeze for 1 month. Reheat channa to 165°F on the stovetop with a splash of water. Warm bara one at a time in a lightly oiled skillet over medium-low for 20 to 30 seconds per side; do not microwave assembled doubles because the bread turns gummy.
notes: Traditional context: Tourism Trinidad describes doubles as fried bara filled with curried channa and commonly finished with tamarind, chadon beni, pepper sauce and cucumber. The name refers to the two overlapping bara used for one serving, not to a double quantity of chickpeas.

Photo-match record: the selected licensed photograph clearly shows turmeric-yellow fried bara under saucy whole chickpeas, with pale cucumber and contrasting chutneys, served on brown paper. Those visible components are all present in this recipe.

Frying-readiness checklist: dough is soft enough to cling slightly to oiled fingers; a stretched round is thin enough to see shadow through it; oil returns to 350°F before each batch; cooked bara bend without cracking; and the surface remains yellow-gold rather than brown.

Twelve-bara batch map: stretch four rounds while the oil heats; fry rounds 1–4; stretch the next four while the oil recovers; fry 5–8; then repeat for 9–12. This prevents the delicate rounds from sitting long enough to stick or overproof.

Texture rescue chart — dough tears: rest 10 minutes longer; dough snaps back: it is under-rested; bara brown before 15 seconds: oil is too hot; bara greasy and flat: oil is too cool; channa runs off the bread: simmer uncovered 2 to 4 minutes; channa sits dry: add hot water 1 tablespoon at a time.

Oil safety: use a stable heavy pot, keep the oil below the halfway mark, lower dough away from your body, keep water and damp utensils away from the pot, and cool the oil completely before straining or disposal.

faqs.q: Why are my bara crisp instead of soft and flexible?
faqs.a: The oil was probably too hot, the dough rounds were too thick, or they fried too long. Keep the oil at 350 to 365°F, stretch each 41 g piece to about 5 inches and remove it as soon as both sides are cooked and lightly puffed. Drain for only 30 seconds, then move it under a clean towel so residual steam preserves flexibility.

faqs.q: Can I make Trinidad doubles without deep-frying?
faqs.a: A skillet version is possible but it will taste more like a soft flatbread than classic bara. Brush a cast-iron skillet lightly with oil and cook thin rounds over medium-high for 30 to 45 seconds per side. They will be less airy and less tender, so serve them immediately and loosen the channa slightly to compensate.

faqs.q: How far ahead can I prepare doubles for a party?
faqs.a: Make the channa and tamarind chutney up to 2 days ahead, then reheat the chickpeas to 165°F. Mix and fry the bara within 2 hours of serving. Hold freshly fried breads under a towel for no more than 30 minutes, and let guests assemble their own doubles so the sauce does not soak through before eating.
